tasks.task_description: Part 1. Build a mathematical model describing the spread and characteristics of reported synthetic-opioid (narcotic analgesic) and heroin drug-identification incidents across the five states (OH, KY, WV, VA, PA) and their counties over 2010-2017; identify where specific opioid use likely started in each state; and, if patterns continue, state the drug-identification threshold levels the U.S. government should watch, and where and when the model predicts they will be crossed.
tasks.task_analysis: The NFLIS 'DrugReports' counts are a *reporting* series, not a prevalence series: an identification enters the data only when local law enforcement seizes evidence and a crime lab tests it. Per the domain expert (Exchange 1), the level of a county's counts is driven mainly by enforcement and submission behavior (task forces, grants, submission thresholds, lab intake policy), while the underlying street supply sets a floor and drives the substance *mix* more reliably than the *level*. Consequence for model design: raw county-year counts cannot be read as prevalence, so the model characterizes dynamics on (a) the state-year substance-class shares (the supply/mix signal, less sensitive to enforcement) and (b) state-year total reported counts (the level, enforcement-sensitive, used only for relative same-state comparisons). A county-year with fewer than N_MIN=10 total narcotic/heroin identifications is flagged low-reliability and excluded from any rate or threshold-crossing claim (Exchange 3: percent changes are meaningless at such counts; a jump from ~0 to a few dozen is a handful of cases, not an epidemic). To separate a genuine 'use started here' signal from an enforcement artifact, a county-year is classified as an EMERGENT origin for a substance class only if it passes a three-part supply-shift test (Exchange 2): (i) the class first reaches a reliable count (>=K_ONS=5) in a mid-window year (>2011, i.e. not already present at the 2010-2011 data start), (ii) the county's class share that year is at least the state's class share that year (composition signal), and (iii) at least one other county in the same state has a reliable count of that class in the adjacent year (regional corroboration, since supply is regional while enforcement is local). Substances are grouped into Fentanyl (fentanyl and all fentanyl analogs and related research chemicals), Heroin, and OtherSynthetic (oxycodone, hydrocodone, methadone, buprenorphine, codeine, and the remaining listed narcotic analgesics). This grouping is defensible because the problem contrasts synthetic opioids vs heroin, and fentanyl is the fast-moving synthetic class whose emergence defines the post-2013 dynamics.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: N(c,t,s) = reported identifications of class s in county c, year t; the class set s in {Fentanyl, Heroin, OtherSynthetic}. Reporting-series decomposition (Exchange 1): N(c,t,s) = e(c,t) * S(c,t,s) * z(c,t), where e(c,t) is an unobserved positive enforcement/submission multiplier, S(c,t,s) is the supply-driven component, and z is multiplicative noise. Because e(c,t) is unobserved and can be agency-linked and reversible (Exchange 2), S is not estimated directly; instead: (1) Mix/supply signal: state-year class share p_s(t) = N_s(t) / sum_{s'} N_{s'}(t), where N_s(t)=sum_c N(c,t,s); trends in p_s(t) are the supply indicator. (2) Level: state-year total T(t)=sum_c sum_s N(c,t,s), fit by a per-state exponential T_s(t) = exp(a_s + b_s (t-2010)) on the 2010-2017 window, R^2 reported per state; used only for relative, same-state, short-horizon (<=2 yr) comparison. (3) Origin detection: for each county c and class s, let t0(c,s) = min{t: N(c,t,s) >= K_ONS, t>2011}; if it exists and share_s(c,t0) >= p_s^state(t0) and exists c'!=c with N(c',t0+delta,s)>=K_ONS for delta in {-1,0,1}, then c is an EMERGENT origin of s at t0. (4) Forward projection: extend the per-state exponential to 2018-2030; a threshold level H is crossed in year t* = ceil((ln H - a_s)/b_s + 2010) when b_s>0. Thresholds reported: 2x the 2010 state total, 2x the 2017 state total, and 5x the 2010 state total. Key empirical inputs (all from the supplied dataset; no external values): class groupings per the substance list in MCM_NFLIS_Data.xlsx; N_MIN=10 and K_ONS=5 are reliability/onsset operating constants set from the expert's low-count guidance (Exchange 3), not empirical prevalence figures. Data cleaning: 24,062 substance-county-year rows, no missing DrugReports, no duplicate (year, FIPS, substance) keys after dedup; substance names trimmed of stray whitespace; 'Other' class (substances outside the three modeled classes) excluded from class shares. Fentanyl group contains 37 named variants (fentanyl, acetyl/butyryl/crotonyl/3-methyl/alpha-/fluoro- etc. analogs, U-47700, U-48800, U-49900, U-51754, MT-45, ANPP, metazocine).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. State-year totals (3 classes) show OH growing fastest (2010: ~20k -> 2017: ~38k, CAGR +0.113, R^2=0.974), PA slower (CAGR +0.049, R^2=0.883), VA weakest fit (CAGR +0.026, R^2=0.334), while KY and WV show slightly *negative* exponential fits (CAGR -0.017 and -0.080) because their totals are volatile and enforcement-sensitive rather than smoothly growing; their 2016-2017 fentanyl jumps are not captured by a smooth exponential, which is exactly why the level model is used only for relative comparison. Class shares (the supply signal) show a consistent, decisive shift in every state: fentanyl share rises from <1% in 2010-2012 to a large fraction of the synthetic mix by 2017 (e.g. OH fentanyl 0.3%->43.1%, Heroin 47.2%->36.1%; PA fentanyl 0.3%->36.0%; VA 0.5%->20.1%; WV 0.3%->19.2%; KY 0.3%->29.3%), while OtherSynthetic (mostly oxycodone/hydrocodone) declines. This is the dominant characteristic: the crisis in these states is a *fentanyl-substitution* event in 2013-2017 layered on an established heroin+oxycodone baseline, not a simple uniform increase. Where use 'started': the emergent-fentanyl origins (three-part test) are, by earliest year, VA (Prince Edward County, 2012; a cluster of northern-Virginia/tidewater cities in 2013: Chesapeake, Norfolk, Virginia Beach, Fairfax, Henrico), then OH and PA in 2013 (Allen, Butler, Mahoning, Montgomery in OH; Berks in PA), and KY and WV in 2014 (Boone, Campbell, Fayette, Kenton, Montgomery in KY; Berkeley, Cabell, Wood in WV). Heroin and OtherSynthetic are 'established' (reliable in 2010-2011) in nearly all counties, so they are not treated as 'started' — the genuine *new* signal is fentanyl, and it appears first in the Virginia corridor and the OH/PA industrial counties, consistent with regional supply routes. Threshold levels and predicted crossing years (exponential on state totals, reliable-window): OH crosses 2x its 2017 total (~83k) around 2023 and 5x its 2010 total (~99k) around 2024; PA crosses 2x-2017 (~55k) around 2030 and 2x-2010 around 2024; VA crosses 2x-2010 around 2030; KY and WV do not cross any of these level thresholds on a smooth fit (their growth is not smoothly exponential). Government concerns: (1) the fentanyl share is the early-warning variable — a sustained rise in fentanyl's share of a state's synthetic mix is the supply signal to act on, ahead of any total-count threshold; (2) total-count thresholds (2x/5x the 2010 or 2017 state totals) are crossed first in OH (2023-2024) and PA (2024), so those states hit level alarms earliest; (3) because the level is enforcement-sensitive, a *drop* in a state's total does not mean the supply fell — it may be reduced submission. Limitations/bias: the model observes identifications, not users; levels are confounded by unobserved enforcement (Exchange 1), so absolute cross-state level comparisons and long-horizon level extrapolation are low-confidence — the fentanyl *share* trend is the more reliable quantity; 16.9% of county-years are below the N_MIN=10 reliability floor and are excluded from threshold claims; the exponential is fit on only 8 annual points and KY/VA/WV fits have low R^2, so crossing years for those states carry wide uncertainty; the background text names five states but the supplied data actually contain five different states (OH, KY, WV, VA, PA, with Pennsylvania in place of Tennessee); the analysis uses the five states present in the data.

tasks.task_description: Part 2. Using the supplied U.S. Census (ACS) socio-economic data, test whether opioid use or trends-in-use is associated with any of the provided socio-economic factors; if so, modify the Part 1 model to include the important factors.
tasks.task_analysis: The ACS DP02 profile tables (one 5-year extract per year 2010-2016, county level) do not contain income, poverty, unemployment, or housing-value fields — the usable county attributes are population, household structure, educational attainment, veteran status, disability, and language. From these I build six county covariates: total population (pop_total), share of adults 25+ with a high-school-or-higher credential (pct_hs), share with a bachelor's degree (pct_bach, computed from counts because the percent columns are (X)-suppressed), share of households where the householder lives alone (living_alone_share), share of the civilian 18+ population that are veterans (veteran_share), and share of the population 5+ speaking English only (en_only_share). Because these are near-time-invariant county attributes, a pooled OLS with state and year dummies alone would attribute all their variation to the dummies (spurious zero coefficients). To recover their marginal effect I estimate a within-county (county fixed effects) level model: log(1+count) = county_FE + year_FE + beta'Z, where Z are the standardized covariates; the covariates' partial R^2 isolates their contribution beyond county and year. I also estimate a trend model regressing each county's 2010->2017 log-growth directly on its 2016 covariates (no FE needed for a single change score). Model modification to Part 1: the supply component S(c,t,s) is allowed to depend on the county's socio-economic profile through a log-linear term, S(c,t,s) proportional to exp(gamma' x_c) where x_c is the standardized ACS vector; this makes the *baseline level* of identifications in a county a function of its socio-economic profile while leaving the fentanyl *share* trend (the supply signal) driven by the state-level dynamics. The key interpretation guard from Exchange 1/3 is retained: these associations describe the reported identification level, not prevalence.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Level model: y_c,t = ln(1+N(c,t)) = alpha_c + lambda_t + sum_k beta_k Z_{c,t,k} + eps, with Z_{c,t,k} the standardized (mean 0, sd 1) ACS covariate k in county c matched to the overlapping ACS year, alpha_c county fixed effects, lambda_t year fixed effects. Estimated by OLS (numpy lstsq) on n=3,480 matched county-years. Partial R^2 for the covariate block = (SS_res[FE-only] - SS_res[full]) / SS_tot. Trend model: delta_c = ln(1+N(c,2017)) - ln(1+N(c,2010)) = sum_k gamma_k Z'_{c,k} + eps, Z' standardized 2016 covariates, n=418 counties. Covariates: pop_total, pct_hs, pct_bach, living_alone_share, veteran_share, en_only_share. Data cleaning: ACS percent columns that are (X)-suppressed are replaced by ratios of the available count columns (e.g. pct_bach = bachelors / educ_pop25); county identifiers are matched on the 5-digit FIPS (NFLIS FIPS_Combined == ACS county id); 3,480 of the county-years matched an ACS extract. All covariate values are from the supplied ACS files; no external values are used.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. Level model (county FE + year FE): full R^2=0.869 vs FE-only R^2=0.865, so the six socio-economic covariates explain a small but nonzero additional share (partial R^2 = 0.0047). Direction of the standardized coefficients: veteran_share is the strongest, negative (-0.335) — counties with a larger share of veterans have *fewer* reported identifications, per-capita; educational attainment is negative (pct_hs -0.167, pct_bach -0.161) — more-educated counties show fewer reported identifications; pop_total is negative (-0.090) — a scale effect (larger counties, after the log and FE, show lower per-capita rate); en_only_share is positive (+0.238) — higher English-only share associates with more reported identifications; living_alone_share is weakly negative (-0.026). Trend model (2010->2017 growth vs 2016 covariates): R^2=0.027, essentially no covariate predicts the *within-county* fentanyl-era growth (pop_total +0.172 is the only nonzero, and it is a scale artifact). Interpretation: the supplied socio-economic profile is associated with the *level* of reported opioid identifications (counties with fewer veterans and lower educational attainment report more, consistent with the well-documented concentration of the crisis in less-educated, non-metro Appalachian counties), but it does NOT predict which counties grow fastest during 2010-2017. The growth is driven by the state-level fentanyl supply signal (Part 1), not by the cross-sectional socio-economic gradient. This is the honest, data-supported answer to 'is use or trend-in-use associated with the Census data': level — yes (modestly); trend — no, not with these variables. Model modification: the Part 1 supply baseline is made profile-dependent, S(c,t,s) ~ exp(gamma' x_c) with gamma from the level model, so the model now places a higher *baseline* identification level in low-veteran/low-education counties while keeping the fentanyl *share* trajectory at the state level. Limitations: the covariates are time-invariant, so their within-county effect over time is identified only through the FE partial R^2, which is small (0.0047) — the socio-economic profile is a modest level shifter, not a growth driver; the trend model's low R^2 (0.027) means we should not over-claim that education or veteran status 'causes' the fentanyl surge; (X)-suppressed percent columns force use of count ratios, which add small measurement error; the ACS 5-year rolling windows overlap and are not perfectly aligned to the NFLIS year, so the level-model covariates carry a lag of up to ~2 years; income/poverty/unemployment, the socio-economic factors most often cited in the literature, are simply absent from the supplied DP02 tables, so the association test is necessarily narrower than the full hypothesis space.

tasks.task_description: Part 3. Using the Part 1 and Part 2 results, identify a strategy for countering the opioid crisis, use the model(s) to test its effectiveness, and identify the significant parameter bounds on which success or failure depends.
tasks.task_analysis: The two results point to a *targeted* rather than uniform strategy. Part 1 shows the actionable, supply-driven signal is the fentanyl emergence in a specific set of counties (the emergent origins), while the level is confounded by enforcement; Part 2 shows the socio-economic profile shifts the baseline level but does not drive the growth. A strategy that sprays resources evenly across all counties would waste effort on (a) the established heroin/oxycodone baseline, which is not the fast-moving threat, and (b) counties whose count changes are enforcement artifacts. The chosen strategy is therefore TARGETED INTERVENTION in the emergent-fentanyl counties: concentrate interdiction of the synthetic supply plus treatment/naloxone demand response in the counties flagged by the Part 1 three-part test, because that is where the real, regionally-corroborated, composition-changing supply signal is. The model represents the intervention as a multiplicative reduction in the supply-driven component in covered counties: N_treated = N_base * (1 - theta*coverage), where theta in [0,1] is the per-county effectiveness (fraction of the supply-driven fentanyl identifications suppressed) and coverage is the fraction of a state's counties that are flagged emergent and therefore reached. This acts on S (supply), consistent with the Part 1 decomposition, so its benefit is concentrated in the fentanyl component and diluted in the established heroin base.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Coverage(s) = (# emergent-fentanyl counties in state s) / (total counties in s), taken from Part 1. The per-state fentanyl volume is projected 2018-2030 by the Part 1 per-state fentanyl exponential fitted on the 2013-2017 emergence window. Baseline cumulative fentanyl identifications B_s = sum_{t=2018}^{2030} exp(a_s + b_s (t-2010)). Treated volume under effectiveness theta and coverage c_s: B_s(theta) = B_s * (1 - theta*c_s). Success is defined as a cumulative reduction of at least 20% in projected fentanyl identifications, i.e. theta*c_s >= 0.20, giving the bound theta >= 0.20 / c_s. Parameters: theta (per-county intervention effectiveness, the free parameter to be bounded) and coverage c_s (determined by how many emergent counties the strategy actually reaches; it is a planning choice as well as a Part 1 output). All inputs (coverage, per-state fentanyl fits, county counts) are from the supplied dataset via Parts 1-2; no external effectiveness figure is assumed — theta is treated as the decision variable and the bound states what value of it is required for success.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. Coverage (fraction of a state's counties flagged as emergent-fentanyl origins by the three-part test): PA 0.61 (41/67), VA 0.47 (61/131), OH 0.38 (33/88), WV 0.35 (19/55), KY 0.27 (32/120). Baseline cumulative fentanyl identifications 2018-2030 (per-state exponential on the 2013-2017 emergence window) are dominated by OH (largest, fastest-growing fentanyl volume) and then PA/KY/WV, with VA smallest. Because the intervention benefit scales as theta*coverage, the same per-county effectiveness buys a bigger state-level cut where coverage is higher, so PA (0.61) needs the lowest required theta and KY (0.27) the highest. Effectiveness at a reference theta=0.30 yields a cumulative fentanyl cut of about 18% in PA, 14% in VA, 11% in OH, 10% in WV, and 8% in KY. Significant parameter bounds (success = >=20% cumulative fentanyl cut): the required per-county effectiveness is theta >= 0.33 in PA, theta >= 0.43 in VA, theta >= 0.53 in OH, theta >= 0.58 in WV, and theta >= 0.75 in KY. These bounds are the key result: in the high-coverage state (PA) a moderate per-county effectiveness (>=0.33) suffices, but in the low-coverage state (KY, coverage 0.27) the strategy fails unless the per-county effectiveness is very high (>=0.75) or coverage is expanded to more counties. Failure modes are therefore (1) low coverage (few emergent counties reached, e.g. KY) and (2) low per-county effectiveness (theta below the bound). Strategy implications: (a) prioritize PA, VA, and OH, where a realistic per-county effectiveness clears the bound; (b) in KY the binding constraint is coverage — expand the set of targeted counties or accept a smaller cut; (c) because the bound is on the *supply* component and Part 1 shows the fentanyl *share* (not the enforcement-driven level) is the real signal, the intervention should be judged on whether it slows the fentanyl-share growth, not on raw total counts; (d) the Part 2 profile (low veteran share, low educational attainment) identifies which counties have the highest baseline burden and should receive the treatment/naloxone arm, but it should not be used to reallocate the supply-interdiction arm, since it does not predict growth. Limitations: theta is a planning parameter, not an empirically estimated effect — no causal effectiveness of a specific intervention is identified from these data, so the bound states the required effectiveness for a 20% cut, not what any real program achieves; the 20% success threshold is an arbitrary planning target and the bound scales linearly with it; the fentanyl exponential is fit on four annual points (2013-2017), so the 2018-2030 baseline volumes carry wide uncertainty and the cumulative cut inherits it; the strategy assumes the emergent set stays roughly the same set of counties, whereas in reality the fentanyl front keeps moving, so coverage must be re-estimated as new origins appear.

tasks.task_description: Deliverable. A 1-2 page memo to the Chief Administrator, DEA/NFLIS Database, summarizing the significant insights and results identified during this modeling effort.
tasks.task_analysis: The memo distills the three parts into the operational points the database administrator needs: what the NFLIS counts do and do not measure, the single early-warning variable, where the fentanyl front first appeared in each state, which states hit level thresholds first, the modest socio-economic level association, and the targeted-intervention bound. It is framed as a reporting-series caveat first, because the database's users are most at risk of misreading raw counts as prevalence.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No additional model; the memo restates, in plain operational terms, the quantities computed in Parts 1-3: (1) the reporting-series caveat N = e*S*z and why raw county counts must not be read as prevalence; (2) the fentanyl-share early-warning indicator and its 2010->2017 trajectory per state; (3) the emergent-fentanyl origin counties by state and year; (4) the level-threshold crossing years per state (2x/5x the 2010 and 2017 totals); (5) the low-count reliability floor (N_MIN=10) and the 16.9% of county-years below it; (6) the socio-economic level coefficients (veteran and education negative, English-only positive) and the finding that they do not predict growth; (7) the targeted-intervention bound theta >= 0.20/coverage with the per-state required effectiveness (PA 0.33, VA 0.43, OH 0.53, WV 0.58, KY 0.75).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Memo to the Chief Administrator, DEA/NFLIS Database. (1) Read the counts as reporting, not prevalence. An identification appears only when local law enforcement seizes and a lab tests evidence. A single aggressive agency can multiply a county's counts with no change in street supply, and a quieter year can shrink counts with no change in use. Do not rank counties or states by raw DrugReports alone. (2) Watch the fentanyl share, not the total. The one reliable, supply-driven signal in these five states is the rising share of fentanyl among reported synthetic opioids: from under 1% in 2010-2012 to roughly 20-43% of the synthetic mix by 2017 in every state (OH 43%, KY 29%, PA 36%, WV 19%, VA 20%). A sustained rise in this share is the early warning to act on; a flat or falling total is not evidence the supply fell. (3) Where the fentanyl front first appeared. Virginia led (Prince Edward County 2012; a northern-VA/tidewater city cluster in 2013), followed by Ohio and Pennsylvania in 2013 (OH: Allen, Butler, Mahoning, Montgomery; PA: Berks) and Kentucky and West Virginia in 2014 (KY: Boone, Campbell, Fayette, Kenton; WV: Berkeley, Cabell, Wood). Heroin and oxycodone-type synthetics were already established statewide in 2010-2011, so the genuinely new signal is fentanyl. (4) Which states hit level thresholds first. On a smooth extrapolation of state totals, Ohio crosses twice its 2017 total around 2023 and five times its 2010 total around 2024; Pennsylvania crosses twice its 2010 total around 2024 and twice its 2017 total around 2030; Virginia around 2030 for twice-2010. Kentucky and West Virginia do not cross these level thresholds on a smooth fit because their totals are volatile and enforcement-sensitive. (5) Reliability floor. County-years with fewer than 10 total narcotic/heroin identifications (16.9% of county-years) are too small to support a rate or threshold claim; treat a jump from near-zero to a few dozen in a single rural county as a reporting signal to verify, not a prevalence finding. (6) Socio-economics shift the level, not the growth. Counties with fewer veterans and less educational attainment report more identifications (veteran share and high-school/bachelor share both negatively associated; English-only share positively), but no supplied socio-economic factor predicts which counties grew fastest 2010-2017 — the growth is the state-level fentanyl supply signal. (7) Counter-strategy and its bound. Concentrate interdiction plus treatment/naloxone in the emergent-fentanyl counties (coverage: PA 0.61, VA 0.47, OH 0.38, WV 0.35, KY 0.27 of counties). To cut projected 2018-2030 fentanyl identifications by at least 20%, the required per-county effectiveness is theta >= 0.33 (PA), 0.43 (VA), 0.53 (OH), 0.58 (WV), 0.75 (KY). Prioritize PA, VA, and OH; in Kentucky the binding constraint is coverage, not per-county effectiveness. The bottom line for the database: instrument the fentanyl share and the low-count reliability flag as first-class fields, because they carry the real signal that raw counts obscure. Limitations: all of the above describes reported identifications, not underlying use; the per-county effectiveness bound is a planning target, not a measured program effect; and the background text names five states but the supplied data actually contain OH, KY, WV, VA, and PA (Pennsylvania in place of Tennessee); the analysis uses the states present in the data.
